chapter: Strings, arrangements and the Shrine band
title: Hearing Robichaux and Perrone, and keeping a winning combination
summary: DeDroit recalls going to hear other bands, his father's advice never to break up a winning combination, and keeping trumpeter Al Hurt in his band thirteen years.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I don't like to talk. I don't have a stick. Sure. I'm curious to know about some of the other orchestras. How would you describe Robichaux and the kind of jobs, what kind of jobs did he get, do you know of, and Perrone? Well, as I told you, I was- You're so busy yourself.

I was so busy that I, but I used to tell Mr. Grimowall and Mr. Cobb that I would like to know what the others are doing. So I'd like a night off once in a while, you see? So I'd go out and see Perrone, and he knew me, and he was a crippling violinist. He wrote, I wish I could shimmy like my sister Kate, you know, and I don't know whether he got credit for it. And I would listen to the bands and see what they're doing, and perhaps if I didn't think it's good enough I wouldn't shimmy. Because my father always told me when I'd get ready to make a change in the band, he said, son, never break up a winning combination. And I had it proven to me so much. One night I had Al Belanco who is now a leader. He was playing second trumpet with me. He's a nice looking fella. He sang well, especially western tunes. He sang like a cowboy and that's all I used him on. He had what I wanted. I was loaded and I was singing. And he was in the hospital and I got the Marion Sutter, whom I consider, I guess the best dance trumpet playing in the city, for me. He had a beautiful style, always played clean, no fuss. He's now an officer of the union. So I was playing up at Reserve and I was very popular in Reserve. I used to pack the joint up. If we wore blue pants and a white coat or a white coat and a blue pants, when we come back the next time all the kids would have the same uniform. You know what I mean? They admired us though. And so Sutter's playing there and I'm really, oh I'm having a good time now. Let me play first. I split the book. And I'm loving the way he plays. The manager comes up and he says, where's Al? I said Al's in the hospital. I'm looking up, where's Al? That's too bad. Tell Al to help me. I said, but you've got Marion Sutter here. I said, Al's in the hospital. He says his first trumpet was the Dawn Busters. You know what, WWL? They used to have the Dawn Busters. Pinky Vinakovich had a fine orchestra. Al Hurt was the first trumpet. They played about, they played nine hours a week for $94 a week. Yeah. They get up about four o'clock in the morning. So I said, that's Marion Sutter. I said, he's helping me out. I said, Al is, I said, he's the best trumpet man in town. He said, that's what you say, I still like Al. Well, I said, I'm glad of that. He liked Al. I went, Al couldn't open the case. Al was a good all-around man. He sang good western tunes and he was handsome. He made a big hit. I kept him in my band for 13 years. I never made any changes because my daddy used to tell me, don't break a winning combination. And I think that's good advice. And I'd hear another drum roll player. I said, I'd like to hang out there. And I think about what my daddy said. And you know that members of your band have their friends too. So you've got to give them all a chance. And like I told you before, when I found out a guy I liked to tune, I featured him. And he played him. There's a lot of psychology.
